name: Bilal Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy parts for Kessler Auto Supply, brake pads, filters, belts, batteries, and I keep around 18,000 different items on the shelves for local garages. I check the sales numbers first thing, then I ring the manufacturers' reps about what's moving. Around noon the garages start calling, and half my job is being the guy who knows what fits a 2011 hatchback. Twenty-seven years, and my team has shrunk from six buyers to three.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being useful. A mechanic rings me stuck with a car on the lift, and I find the part in two minutes. What wears me out is the paperwork and the way the sales targets move every quarter. My wife Nadia dispatches school buses, so our evenings are mostly spent comparing who had the worse day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. I use a chat tool now and then to translate part numbers between brands, and it saves me ten minutes. Not life-changing. I'd tell the lads in the warehouse not to lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm uneasy more than calm. Nadia and I have about three weeks of money in the bank, and our daughter Soraya's wedding is next summer. Even with nothing changing, I'm counting every note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and use the tool a little more. I'd ask the boss, Gerhard, whether we can get a raise at the next review. I'd put aside 80 a month for the wedding. And I'd say yes if my brother-in-law offers me the Saturday shifts at his garage counter again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. My situation is like driving a car with a warning light on. The car runs, but you listen to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the warning light is the wedding. How would that conversation with Soraya go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warning light is the wedding and the thin savings. If Soraya asks for more help, I'd tell her honestly we can do 3,000, not 8,000. She'd understand, but I'd hate saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by fewer promises and more action?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody to blame, really. It's the way costs go up. Politicians talk a lot and wages stay put. I'd want fewer promises and more action on rent and food prices.

I'd tell the warehouse lads not to **lose sleep**.

Even with nothing changing, I'm counting every note.
do: Use the chat tool a little more for **part-number** matching.
Put aside **80 a month** for the wedding.
Take the Saturday shifts at my brother-in-law's **garage counter**.
feel: Mostly fine, but like a car with a **warning light** on.

fieldNote: His job looks safe, but a thin **cushion** and a wedding bill keep him uneasy.
Blames nothing in particular; wants **politicians** to deliver instead of talk.
The **warning-light** image is an honest summary of his state.

steps.text: Use the chat tool to match part numbers across brands
Put aside 80 a month for Soraya's wedding
Take Saturday shifts at my brother-in-law's garage counter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already started. We cut from six buyers to three over six years and it wasn't the robots. It was software that suggests the order and lets one person do the work of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm one of the three, and I'm 58. If it goes to two I know who the target is, and it isn't the 31-year-old who learns everything in a weekend. I'd be hard to defend on cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, not just the part-number trick. The distributor runs a course, and I'd sign up even though it eats an evening a week. I'd make myself the person that garages ask for by name, so the sales team fights to keep me. And I'd ask Nadia to double-check our budget, because I think we can find 200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, like waiting to see if my number comes up. But I'm trying to do something about it, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the call with Mr. Okafor. Why does that matter to your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month Mr. Okafor, a garage owner, rang me instead of using the online page. The page had given Mr. Okafor the wrong brake disc, and I fixed it in two minutes. That's the sort of thing I'd use to show I'm worth the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd blame yourself a bit. What would you have done differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they cut me, I'd blame myself a bit and the owners a bit. But mostly I'd say that's how business works. It doesn't make it easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's scary and fast, and I'd say it's going to hit places like ours early. Parts buying is about numbers and phone calls. Both are what the AI does well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's gone, or cut to one person who checks the system's work. I'd be 60. I'd have a wife with a stable job, which is a mercy, but our savings wouldn't last a season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Gerhard right away and ask where he sees me. Then I'd apply for the warehouse team lead job, since hands-on work lasts about three years longer. I'd take every Saturday shift at my brother-in-law's garage. I'd also postpone Soraya's big wedding and go small, which I'd hate to do. And I'd look at the government retraining list, because I'm not too proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and not sleeping well. I make jokes at work, but it's a mask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make jokes at work as a mask. Who knows how you really feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Soraya and say, look, we've got to scale it down. She'd cry and then she'd understand. It's the sort of thing I'd have to say to my own child, and I hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a government to have done years ago?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no one's fault, but someone should have been working on this years ago. Governments and companies knew AI was coming and did nothing. That's what I'd say if I were asked at an election.

say: I'd say it's **scary and fast**, and places like ours will be hit early.
I'd say governments and companies knew it was coming and did **nothing**.
think: I think my job is gone, or cut to one person **checking** the system.
Nadia's stable job is a mercy, but our savings wouldn't last a **season**.

Apply for the **warehouse team lead** job, since hands-on work lasts about 3 years longer.
Cut Soraya's wedding down to a **small** one.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleeping badly, with jokes at work as a mask.
S2.quote: I'd sit down with Soraya and say, look, we've got to scale it down. She'd cry and then she'd understand.
fieldNote: **Expects** the buyer role to vanish; his wife's steady job is the only buffer.

steps.text: Ask Gerhard in person where he sees me in two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent head start. It's like a long road with a slow-moving truck ahead: you see it, you plan your overtake. I'd tell the team to use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63. I think I could ride it out, but it'd be close. I'd want a plan that gets me to 65 with a small pension, and I think Nadia's pension helps there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the software course in the first year, then try to move into account management, looking after the big garages. That's a human job for longer. I'd save 250 a month toward the wedding and retirement. I'd talk to Soraya early so the wedding budget is realistic. And I'd keep the Saturday shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. This is the one where I think I'd hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said account management is a human job for longer. What makes you think so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd watch is whether the firm keeps anyone my age. If Gerhard says in year two that buyer jobs are going, I'd start applying elsewhere, even if it's an hour's drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start applying elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it fails, I'd rather leave with something in the bank than get pushed out with nothing. That's why I'd save now, while I still can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, that's a long runway. I'd say don't panic, plan, and I'd tell the young ones to find something hands-on. For me, I'd be nearly done anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68. I'd plan to stop at 65, with Nadia's pension and whatever I've saved. I think it works, though only if I start saving now. The weak point is the savings, not the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 65, keep the weekend shifts and pay off the credit card. I'd save 150 a month and top up my pension. I'd help Soraya with a deposit, if I can. And I'd keep learning the tools in the meantime, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the first one where I think we'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd plan for a deposit for Soraya. What could you realistically offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would worry me is if prices jump, because ten years of my careful saving wouldn't cover that. It's a car with a good engine, but I don't know the price of fuel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who worries you most among the people you work with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the government to guarantee the state pension and fund retraining. Not for me, for the lads who are 40 and have kids in school.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years, 60 years old, three weeks of savings. What would help is a retraining list that actually leads to work, a state pension that stays put, and a boss who tells me early. And maybe a wedding that doesn't cost the earth.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of the tools. I'm scared of the schedule. If somebody told me what the plan is, I'd work with it.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the tools. I'm scared of the schedule. If somebody told me what the plan is, I'd work with it.
portrait: **Bilal Wagner**, 58, buys car parts for a supply firm and has seen his buying team shrink from six to three.
He is **centre** and steady: he uses AI tools now and then, jokes to cover worry, and blames nobody in particular.
A thin cushion and his daughter's wedding keep him **uneasy**, and he turns **anxious** or alarmed when buyer jobs look at risk.
His wife Nadia's school-bus dispatch job and pension are a steady anchor.
He would learn the tools, move to **account management**, work Saturdays at a garage and scale back the wedding.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because two years leaves little room and savings would last only a season.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining** list that leads to real work, a steady state pension and early honesty from his boss.
A **wedding** that doesn't cost the earth.
